questions.stem: Economic development differs from economic growth because development refers to:
options: an increase in the volume of goods and services produced in a year
an increase in a country's population and the size of its labour force
a rise in the general level of prices across the whole economy
broad gains in wellbeing, such as in health, education and sustainability
questions.explanation: Growth is a rise in real GDP, while development is a wider improvement in quality of life. A country can grow without developing if the gains are narrow or damage health and the environment.

questions.stem: As countries develop, their economic structure typically changes from:
options: services towards agriculture, and then towards manufacturing
agriculture towards manufacturing, and then towards services
services towards manufacturing, and then towards agriculture
manufacturing towards agriculture, and then towards mining
questions.explanation: Labour moves from low-productivity farming into industry and then into services as incomes rise. Advanced economies such as Australia have most of their workforce in services.

questions.stem: Inclusive growth is best described as growth that:
options: includes the value of unpaid work and volunteering in measured GDP
spreads its benefits widely, including to the poorest households
raises real GDP as fast as possible regardless of how it is shared
relies on exports of natural resources to include the world market
questions.explanation: Inclusive growth raises incomes and opportunities for most people, not just a few, which supports long-term wellbeing. Sustainable growth adds the requirement that it does not degrade the environment for future generations.

questions.stem: Country X's real GDP grows by 7% a year for a decade, but income inequality widens sharply and air pollution causes rising rates of illness. The best assessment is that:
options: strong development has occurred because real GDP has grown rapidly
development has occurred but growth has been weak over the decade
neither growth nor development has occurred in Country X
rapid growth has not produced equally strong economic development
questions.explanation: Growth is necessary for development but not sufficient. When gains are concentrated and health and the environment suffer, wellbeing improves far less than GDP suggests.

questions.stem: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines measures of:
options: income inequality, poverty and the Gini coefficient
life expectancy, education and income per person
GDP growth, inflation and the unemployment rate
exports, imports and the current account balance
questions.explanation: The HDI covers a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean and expected years of schooling) and a decent standard of living (GNI per capita in PPP terms).

questions.stem: Why is GDP per capita converted using purchasing power parity (PPP) when comparing living standards between countries?
options: Price levels differ, so market exchange rates misstate what incomes can buy
Exchange rates are fixed by the IMF, so they cannot reflect differences in income
Population sizes differ, so total GDP must be divided by the number of residents
Inflation is zero in advanced economies, so their GDP need not be adjusted
questions.explanation: Many goods and services, especially non-traded ones, are much cheaper in poorer countries, so converting at market exchange rates understates their real incomes. Dividing by population gives per capita figures, a separate adjustment.

questions.stem: Country A's GDP per capita is $US2,000 at market exchange rates, but $US6,000 in PPP terms. This suggests that in Country A:
options: the general price level is much higher than in the United States
the currency is overvalued at the market exchange rate
living standards are lower than the market rate figure shows
the general price level is much lower than in the United States
questions.explanation: A PPP figure three times the market-rate figure means each dollar of income buys far more in Country A than its exchange rate implies, because local prices are low. Living standards are higher, not lower, than the market-rate figure suggests.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of the HDI as a measure of development?
options: It adjusts income for prices, which makes comparisons less accurate
It leaves out inequality, sustainability and political freedom
It measures only income and ignores health and education completely
It cannot be calculated for developing countries with low incomes
questions.explanation: The HDI uses national averages of three dimensions, so it misses how wellbeing is distributed, environmental damage and freedoms. Variants such as the inequality-adjusted HDI try to address part of this.

questions.stem: Which group of countries has the lowest levels of income and human development, as classified by the United Nations?
options: newly industrialised economies
least developed countries
emerging economies
advanced economies
questions.explanation: The UN classifies least developed countries using low income, weak human assets and high economic vulnerability. Emerging economies are growing and industrialising rapidly from a middle-income base.

questions.stem: An emerging economy is best described as one that:
options: is industrialising rapidly and trading more with world markets
has high incomes, mature institutions and a large service sector
has the lowest incomes in the world and relies heavily on aid
has stopped growing after reaching the limits of its resources
questions.explanation: Emerging economies, such as India, Indonesia and Brazil, combine rapid growth with rising trade and investment links. High incomes and mature institutions describe advanced economies.

questions.stem: Compared with advanced economies, developing countries typically have:
options: a larger share of employment in services and higher life expectancy
older populations and slower rates of population growth
higher average years of schooling and lower birth rates
a larger share of employment in agriculture and lower life expectancy
questions.explanation: Lower productivity, more agricultural employment and weaker health systems are common features of developing economies. Ageing populations and low birth rates are typical of advanced economies.

questions.stem: Economists often argue that strong institutions are a key factor in development. Which is an example of a strong institution?
options: A tropical climate suited to growing a wide range of crops
A young and rapidly growing population of working age
Courts that enforce contracts and property rights fairly
A large reserve of oil that can be exported to world markets
questions.explanation: Institutions are the rules and organisations that govern economic life, such as the rule of law, secure property rights and low corruption. Oil reserves and climate are natural endowments, not institutions.

questions.stem: A landlocked country with few natural resources has grown slowly. Which explanation draws on geography and natural resource endowment?
options: High transport costs to reach ports limit its trade
Widespread corruption discourages businesses from investing there
Low school completion rates leave the workforce with few skills
Weak courts mean that contracts cannot be enforced reliably
questions.explanation: Being landlocked raises the cost of moving goods to and from the coast, limiting trade and specialisation. Corruption and weak courts are institutional factors, and low schooling is a human capital factor.

questions.stem: Investment in schooling and health raises a developing country's long-run growth mainly by:
options: improving the quality of human capital and so labour productivity
increasing the stock of natural resources available for export
lowering the exchange rate so that its exports become cheaper
reducing the need for physical infrastructure such as roads
questions.explanation: Healthier, better-educated workers are more productive and adapt more readily to new technology. Infrastructure, such as roads, power and water, complements rather than replaces human capital.

questions.stem: Some countries rich in oil or minerals have grown more slowly than resource-poor neighbours. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: Natural resources cannot be exported, so they add nothing to measured GDP
Resource-rich countries cannot borrow overseas to invest in infrastructure
Resource wealth has fed corruption and weak institutions, crowding out other industries
Resource wealth has raised human capital so much that wages are too high to compete
questions.explanation: The so-called resource curse links resource wealth to rent-seeking, conflict and a high exchange rate that crowds out other industries. Strong institutions, as in Norway or Australia, help avoid it.

questions.stem: Why does climate change raise global equity issues?
options: Developing countries gain from climate change because their growing seasons lengthen
Poorer countries face large costs although they have contributed little to emissions
Advanced economies face all of the costs because they have the highest emissions
Every country faces equal costs because emissions mix evenly in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Low-income countries are often more exposed to droughts, floods and sea-level rise and have less capacity to adapt, yet their historical emissions are small. This underlies calls for climate finance from wealthier countries.

questions.stem: Pacific island nations argue that advanced economies should fund adaptation measures in their countries. Their economic argument is mainly that:
options: they would gain a comparative advantage in carbon-intensive manufacturing
adaptation spending would raise the world price of their exports
they bear the external costs of emissions produced mostly by others
they have caused most global emissions through their tourism industries
questions.explanation: Greenhouse emissions are a global negative externality: the countries that emit most do not bear the full cost, which falls heavily on low-lying, low-emitting nations. Compensation and climate finance are ways to address this inequity.

questions.stem: Absolute poverty means:
options: being in the lowest fifth of the income distribution of a country
lacking the income to meet basic needs such as food and shelter
having an income below half the median income in one's own country
earning less than the national minimum wage in a full-time job
questions.explanation: Absolute poverty is measured against a fixed standard of basic needs, such as the World Bank's international poverty line. Income below a share of the median is relative poverty.

questions.stem: Over recent decades, the share of the world's population living in extreme poverty has:
options: fallen greatly, led by rapid growth in East Asia, especially China
risen greatly, led by slow growth in East Asia, especially China
stayed roughly constant, as population growth offset income growth
fallen greatly, led mainly by growth in the advanced economies
questions.explanation: Rapid growth in China and the rest of East Asia lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty from the 1990s. Progress has been much slower in parts of sub-Saharan Africa.

questions.stem: Where in the world are most people in extreme poverty now concentrated?
options: Sub-Saharan Africa
East Asia and the Pacific
Latin America
Eastern Europe
questions.explanation: As East Asia's poverty rates fell, extreme poverty became concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, where growth has been slower and population growth faster. Conflict and climate shocks have added to the problem.

questions.stem: The main role of the World Bank Group is to:
options: lend to countries facing short-term balance of payments crises
negotiate tariff reductions and settle disputes between members
set interest rates for central banks in developing countries
reduce poverty by financing development in developing countries
questions.explanation: The World Bank Group provides loans, grants, investment and advice for development projects and reforms. Short-term crisis lending is the IMF's main role, and trade rules are the WTO's.

questions.stem: Within the World Bank Group, the International Development Association (IDA) mainly:
options: insures foreign investors against political risk in host countries
settles investment disputes between governments and foreign firms
gives grants and low-interest loans to the poorest countries
lends to private businesses investing in developing countries
questions.explanation: IDA serves the poorest countries on concessional terms. The IFC invests in the private sector, MIGA provides political risk insurance and ICSID settles investment disputes.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest criticism of the World Bank's effectiveness in achieving development?
options: It sets the exchange rates of developing countries, which has made their exports dearer
It is controlled entirely by developing countries, so donor countries have no say
Some loan conditions hurt the poor, and some projects displaced local communities
It has never lent to any developing country for infrastructure or social programs
questions.explanation: Critics point to structural adjustment conditions in the 1980s and 1990s and to projects such as large dams that displaced communities. Voting power is weighted towards major shareholders such as the US, not developing countries.

questions.stem: Which factor makes Australia especially vulnerable to fluctuations in the Chinese economy?
options: The Australian dollar is pegged to the Chinese yuan
A large share of Australia's resource exports is sold to China
Most of Australia's imported food is produced in China
China holds most of the Australian Government's debt
questions.explanation: China is Australia's largest trading partner and the main buyer of its iron ore, so slower Chinese growth reduces export volumes and prices. The dollar floats; it is not pegged to the yuan.

questions.stem: Australia's reliance on foreign capital to fund investment makes it vulnerable mainly because:
options: foreign investors are legally allowed to take control of the Reserve Bank of Australia
foreign capital must be repaid within one year, regardless of global conditions
foreign capital is the only source of funds for Australian households and firms
a shift in global financial conditions can raise borrowing costs or cut inflows
questions.explanation: Australian banks have long borrowed overseas, so turmoil in world credit markets, as in 2008, can quickly raise their funding costs. National saving also funds investment, so foreign capital is not the only source.

questions.stem: Why are Australia's export earnings more volatile than those of many other advanced economies?
options: Exports are priced in Australian dollars, so they cannot change
Exports are concentrated in commodities, whose prices swing widely
Exports are concentrated in services, whose prices swing widely
Exports are spread evenly across many products and many markets
questions.explanation: Iron ore, coal, gas and other commodities dominate Australia's exports, and their world prices move sharply with global demand. This drives large swings in the terms of trade and national income.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Australian economy helps it absorb external shocks?
options: A heavy reliance on one export market for most of its trade
A floating exchange rate that tends to fall when commodity prices fall
A fixed exchange rate that stays the same when commodity prices fall
High tariffs that prevent overseas downturns from affecting imports
questions.explanation: A falling dollar cushions a negative shock by making exports and import-competing goods more competitive. Reliance on one market increases vulnerability rather than resilience.

questions.stem: Australia avoided a deep recession during the global financial crisis of 2008-09. Which combination of factors best explains this?
options: Falling Chinese demand, an appreciating dollar and cuts to government spending
A rise in unemployment that lowered wages and made exports more competitive
Fiscal stimulus, cash rate cuts, sound banks and continued Chinese demand
Rising interest rates, a budget surplus, high tariffs and a fixed exchange rate
questions.explanation: The RBA cut the cash rate sharply, the government spent on stimulus, well-regulated banks stayed sound and China's stimulus kept demand for resources strong. The dollar's fall also helped.

questions.stem: A strong system of prudential regulation of banks increases Australia's resilience mainly by:
options: requiring banks to lend to every household that applies for a loan
reducing the risk of bank failures when global conditions worsen
guaranteeing that the Australian dollar will not fall in a crisis
preventing Australian banks from borrowing any funds from overseas
questions.explanation: Requirements for capital and liquidity, overseen by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, make banks better able to withstand shocks. They do not stop the dollar moving or ban offshore borrowing.

questions.stem: A government with low public debt relative to other advanced economies is more resilient to external shocks because it:
options: has more room to use fiscal stimulus without threatening its credit rating
can set its exchange rate at any level it chooses during a downturn
does not need to collect taxes while global conditions remain weak
is protected from changes in world commodity prices and export demand
questions.explanation: Low debt gives fiscal space: the government can borrow to support demand in a downturn at reasonable cost. It does not control the floating exchange rate or insulate the economy from export shocks.

questions.stem: Rapid industrialisation in China in the 2000s and 2010s affected the structure of Australia's economy mainly by:
options: expanding manufacturing as the share of employment in factories rose
shrinking the services sector to a minority of total employment
expanding agriculture to become Australia's largest export sector
expanding mining output and investment relative to other industries
questions.explanation: Strong demand for iron ore, coal and gas raised commodity prices, mining investment and the mining share of output. A higher dollar also pressured manufacturing, continuing its long-term decline.

questions.stem: A sharp recession among Australia's major trading partners is most likely to cause in Australia:
options: lower export demand and growth, higher unemployment and a weaker dollar
higher export demand and growth, lower unemployment and a stronger dollar
higher inflation, as overseas producers raise prices for imported goods
no change in growth, because Australia's exports are mainly services
questions.explanation: Falling demand overseas reduces Australian exports and commodity prices, slowing growth and employment. The dollar usually falls, which partly cushions the shock.

questions.stem: Global supply disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic affected the Australian economy mainly by:
options: increasing Australia's dependence on services exports such as tourism
ending Australia's trade with Asia for the duration of the pandemic
raising prices for imported goods and contributing to higher inflation
lowering prices for imported goods and contributing to deflation
questions.explanation: Shortages of goods and higher shipping costs pushed up import prices, adding to inflation that peaked in 2022. Tourism and international education exports fell sharply while borders were closed.

questions.stem: Which policy would most improve Australia's resilience to a fall in demand from one major trading partner?
options: Concentrating exports further on iron ore to the largest existing trading partner
Fixing the exchange rate so that it cannot fall when export demand weakens
Raising tariffs so that Australian firms rely only on the domestic market
Diversifying exports and markets through trade agreements with other countries
questions.explanation: A wider range of products and markets spreads risk, so a shock in one market has a smaller effect. Fixing the dollar would remove a shock absorber, and high tariffs would reduce efficiency.

questions.stem: An external shock is best described as:
options: a change in domestic interest rates announced by the central bank
an increase in domestic government spending in the federal Budget
a change in domestic tastes that shifts demand for local products
an event originating overseas that affects the domestic economy
questions.explanation: External shocks include global recessions, financial crises, pandemics and commodity price swings. Changes in the cash rate or the Budget are domestic policy decisions.

questions.stem: The World Bank's international poverty line is used to measure:
options: relative poverty within Australia
income inequality using the Gini
unemployment in poorer countries
absolute poverty across countries
questions.explanation: The international poverty line is a fixed amount per person per day in PPP dollars, so it measures absolute poverty consistently across countries. Relative poverty in Australia is measured against median income, such as the OECD poverty line.

questions.stem: Australia's largest trading partner is:
options: the United Kingdom
China
the United States
Japan
questions.explanation: China has been Australia's largest two-way trading partner since 2007 and is the main market for its iron ore. Japan and the United States are also major partners.
